Discover Board Game Arena Rules summary Contents 1 Introduction 2 Three vs Four Player Game 3 Cards 4 Round Structure 5 Dealing 5.1 Three Player Cards 5.2 Four Player Cards 6 Bidding 6.1 Three Player Bidding 6.2 Four Player Bidding 7 Trick Structure 7.1 Scoring a Trick 7.2 Resolving Trick Ties 7.3 Round End 8 Scoring a round 8.1 Points for Tricks Taken 8.2 Points for Gold Cards 8.3 Resolving Round Ties 9 Game End 10 Game Options 11 Expert Variant Introduction In Aurum, players take the role of alchemists melding base metals into gold. Aurum is a competitive, trick taking game where players must not follow the suits of previously played base metal cards. Three vs Four Player Game With three players, players play individually. With four players, players play in two teams of two with each player sat between their opponents and opposite the player on their team in clockwise order of play. Cards There are two types of cards in Aurum: • Base Metal Cards are dealt to each player's hand at the start of each round. They are used for playing to tricks and to indicate the number of tricks a player thinks they (or their team) will win during a round. The base metal suits are: Bismuth, Copper, Phosphorus, Silver and Zinc. The cards in player’s hand is private information known only to them and not shared with other players including their partner. • Gold Cards can be played as a trump that always beats base metal cards when played to a trick. Gold cards can be spent to swap players' bids between tricks. Gold cards indicate a number of points they are worth when kept till the end of a round with gold symbols below the number indicating their rank. If a player played the lowest base metal card in a trick, they win a gold card of the same number (rank), if available in the gold supply. There are 2 copies each of gold cards numbered 1, 2 and 3 worth 1 point each at the end of a round; 1 copy each of 4, 5 and 6 worth 2 points; 1 copy each of 7 and 8 worth 3 points each. There are four 0 gold cards worth 0 points given to each player at the start of each round in the base game. Gold cards a player holds are kept publicly in front of a player face up in their gold collection. Round Structure Aurum plays in 2-4 rounds. At the end of each round, one or more players win a gold nugget. A player (or team) with two gold nuggets wins the game. A round consists of the following phases: • Dealing where base metal cards are dealt evenly to players and gold is returned to the supply. Each player receives a 0 gold card. • Bidding where players predict the number of tricks they will win with a card from their hand. • Playing Tricks where each player plays one card. The highest card wins the trick. The lowest base metal card wins a gold card and starts the next trick. • Scoring where the player (or team) with the highest points wins a gold nugget. Points are based on tricks and gold cards won. • Pass on the Round First Player Marker where the marker of which player starts the next round is passed clockwise to the next player. Dealing Each player receives a 0 gold card at the start of each round (except in the Expert Variant). This card is placed face up in front of a player in their gold collection. Three Player Cards With three players, there are four base metal suits with ranks 1-9 . These base metal cards are shuffled and dealt evenly face down between the three players at the beginning of each round. The gold supply contains all gold cards from 1-7 at the start of each round. Four Player Cards With four players, there are five base metal suits with ranks 1-10 and all gold cards in the gold supply from 1-8 at the start of each round. [Rating: 3/10] I think must-not-follow really just isn't my thing. Evaluating the strength of your hand in order to bid is difficult, evaluating the strength of the many cards you have to choose from each turn is difficult, and the fact that ties are awarded to players later in the trick leads to a lot of either indecision or indifference for everybody but the last player in each trick, who often gets unintentionally limited or hosed by the arbitrary decisions of the players ahead of them. Overall, does not have the feeling of effortless flow and subtle control that superior trick-takers are able to provide 

[Rating: 4/10] Meh...I'm still not sure where one's control is here. You really want to the last player to have more control and you have least control as the first player. Uses Potato Man rules for playing card.

[Rating: 4/10] Bidding felt unnecessary as everyone would go 3-5. Game was interesting, but slow.

There are 5 colour suits, with gold being a special 6th suit. Last-played highest card wins the trick and last played lowest card gets a matching gold card, if still available.
